name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Protection of tender root apex during penetration

questiontext.text: Which structure covers the apex of the root to protect its tender apex as it makes its way through the soil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Root Anatomy
The root apex is covered at the very tip by a protective, thimble-like structure.

Step 2: Functional Significance
As the root pushes through rough abrasive soil particles, this thimble-like root cap shields the tender meristematic tissue at the apex from mechanical damage.

Final Answer: The root cap protects the tender root apex as it penetrates the soil.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Origin of fine delicate epidermal root hairs

questiontext.text: Root hairs that absorb water and minerals from the soil arise as fine, delicate thread-like structures from which region of the root?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Zonation of the Root Tip
A growing root exhibits distinct proximal-to-distal zones: root cap, region of meristematic activity, region of elongation, and region of maturation.

Step 2: Epidermal Differentiation
In the region of maturation, the epidermal cells differentiate and produce fine, delicate extensions termed root hairs that increase surface area for absorption of water and minerals.

Final Answer: Root hairs develop from the epidermal cells of the region of maturation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Embryonic origin of the ascending shoot axis

questiontext.text: In a germinating seed, the ascending part of the plant axis, the stem, develops directly from which part of the embryo?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Embryonic Axis Differentiation
During seed germination, the embryonal axis differentiates into two primary poles: the radicle and the plumule.

Step 2: Organogenesis
The radicle elongates to form the primary root system, whereas the plumule develops into the ascending shoot axis bearing stems, leaves, and branches.

Final Answer: The stem develops from the plumule of the embryo of a germinating seed.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Arrangement pattern of veins within leaf lamina

questiontext.text: What term defines the arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina of a leaf?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Leaf Terminology
Different botanical terms describe arrangements of various plant organs: phyllotaxy refers to leaf arrangement on the stem, aestivation refers to floral petal/sepal arrangement in bud, and placentation refers to ovule arrangement.

Step 2: Identification of Venation
The specific pattern and arrangement of veins and veinlets across the leaf lamina is defined as venation.

Final Answer: The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the leaf lamina is termed venation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Palmately compound leaf structure in silk cotton

questiontext.text: Which type of leaf is characteristic of the silk cotton plant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Types of Compound Leaves
In compound leaves, the lamina is divided into distinct leaflets. In pinnately compound leaves, leaflets attach along an elongated common axis (rachis).

Step 2: Attachment in Silk Cotton
In palmately compound leaves, such as in silk cotton, multiple leaflets are articulated and attached at a single common point at the tip of the petiole.

Final Answer: Silk cotton possesses palmately compound leaves.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Growth pattern of cymose floral axis termination

questiontext.text: In a cymose inflorescence, what is the fate and growth pattern of the main floral axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Inflorescence Classification Principle
Inflorescences are categorized into racemose and cymose based on the developmental fate of the shoot apical meristem.

Step 2: Cymose Inflorescence Characteristics
In cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates directly into a flower, restricting further apical elongation, and subsequent flowers are produced in a basipetal sequence.

Final Answer: In a cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower and displays limited growth.

answer.text: The main axis terminates in a flower and has limited growth
The main axis continues to grow indefinitely bearing flowers acropetally
The main axis forms a vegetative runner
The main axis produces flowers solely from root meristems

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Undifferentiated non reproductive perianth whorl in lily

questiontext.text: In flowers of lily, where the calyx and corolla are not distinct, the non-reproductive envelope is termed as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Accessory Floral Organs
In many angiosperms, calyx and corolla form two distinct concentric accessory whorls.

Step 2: Perianth Morphology
When sepals and petals are undifferentiated in appearance and fused into a single collective envelope, as observed in lily flowers, it is termed a perianth.

Final Answer: The non-distinct calyx and corolla whorl in lily is termed perianth.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Structural definition of sterile stamen staminode

questiontext.text: What is a sterile, non-functional stamen called in flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structure of the Androecium
The male reproductive whorl consists of stamens, each typically having a fertile anther and a filament.

Step 2: Sterile Stamen Definition
When a stamen fails to produce viable pollen and becomes sterile, it is specifically designated as a staminode.

Final Answer: A sterile stamen is termed a staminode.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Biological definition of the true angiosperm fruit

questiontext.text: Botanically, what is a true fruit in flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Origin of Angiosperm Fruit
Following pollination and fertilisation, the floral reproductive organs undergo post-fertilisation changes.

Step 2: Morphological Definition
The ovary enlarges, ripens, and differentiates its wall into a pericarp enclosing seeds, defining the fruit as a mature or ripened ovary developed after fertilisation.

Final Answer: A fruit is a mature or ripened ovary developed after fertilisation.

answer.text: A mature or ripened ovary developed after fertilisation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Shield shaped single cotyledon of monocot seed

questiontext.text: In monocotyledonous seeds such as maize, what is the single, large, shield-shaped cotyledon called?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Monocotyledonous Embryo Morphology
The embryo of a monocotyledonous seed consists of a short embryonal axis and a single, lateral cotyledon.

Step 2: Identification of Scutellum
This massive, shield-shaped food-absorbing cotyledon located adjacent to the endosperm is specifically called the scutellum.

Final Answer: The single shield-shaped cotyledon of a monocot embryo is called the scutellum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Pathway of curly top virus spread in plants

questiontext.text: According to the historical contributions of Katherine Esau, through which specific plant tissue does the curly top virus spread across an infected plant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Botanical Research Context
Katherine Esau carried out pioneering research on plant anatomy and viral pathology in agricultural crops.

Step 2: Tissue Pathway of Curly Top Virus
Her early investigations conclusively revealed that the curly top virus moves systemically through the plant via the phloem, the food-conducting vascular tissue.

Final Answer: The curly top virus spreads through the phloem (food-conducting tissue).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Characteristics and example of tap root system

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly describes the formation and an example of a tap root system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Development of the Tap Root
In most dicotyledonous plants, germination involves the continuous direct elongation of the embryonic radicle into the soil as the primary root.

Step 2: Branching and Model Plant
The primary root produces successive lateral branches of secondary and tertiary orders; this architecture is typified by the mustard plant.

Final Answer: The tap root system arises from the direct elongation of the radicle bearing lateral roots, as in mustard.

answer.text: Direct elongation of the radicle forms the primary root bearing lateral roots, as seen in mustard
Short-lived primary root replaced by tufts from the stem base, as seen in wheat
Roots arising adventitiously from nodes of hanging stems, as seen in banyan
Fibrous clusters emerging directly from petiole bases, as seen in Monstera

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q13 - Origin and structure of fibrous root system

questiontext.text: In monocotyledonous plants such as wheat, how does the fibrous root system originate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Monocot Root Ontogeny
In monocots, the primary root formed from the radicle does not persist for a prolonged period and ceases growth early.

Step 2: Fibrous System Architecture
A large number of thin roots arise in clusters from the lower nodes or base of the stem, forming the fibrous root system characteristic of wheat.

Final Answer: The fibrous root system develops when the short-lived primary root is replaced by numerous roots arising from the base of the stem.

answer.text: The primary root is short-lived and replaced by roots originating from the base of the stem
The radicle continues to elongate into a persistent thick taproot
Lateral roots arise exclusively from the petiole and floral stalk
The hypocotyl swells into a permanent tuber bearing adventitious hairs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Occurrence and definition of adventitious root systems

questiontext.text: Roots that arise from parts of the plant other than the embryonic radicle are termed adventitious roots. In which group of plants are adventitious roots found?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Concept of Adventitious Roots
Roots developing from any vegetative plant organ other than the radicle (such as stems, branches, or nodes) are classified as adventitious roots.

Step 2: Representative Examples
Such roots are prominently observed arising from stem nodes and aerial shoots in grass, Monstera, and the banyan tree.

Final Answer: Adventitious roots occur in grass, Monstera, and the banyan tree.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q15 - Primary physiological functions of the root system

questiontext.text: Which combination represents the major functions performed by the root system of a flowering plant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physiological Roles of Roots
The root system provides multiple vital functions essential for vegetative and reproductive plant success.

Step 2: Core Functional Roles
These include absorbing water and dissolved minerals from the soil, providing firm structural anchorage, storing reserve nutrients, and synthesizing endogenous plant growth regulators.

Final Answer: The root system functions in absorption, anchorage, food storage, and synthesis of plant growth regulators.

answer.text: Absorption of water and minerals, anchorage, storage of reserve food, and synthesis of plant growth regulators
Conducting transpiration pull, leaf blade expansion, and producing sexual gametes
Photosynthetic carbon fixation, floral bud differentiation, and guttation
Photoperiodic perception, secondary wall lignification, and seed dispersal

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q16 - Growth in length at root elongation zone

questiontext.text: Which region of the root tip lies proximal to the meristematic activity zone and is directly responsible for the rapid growth of the root in length?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Positional Layout of Root Apex
Directly behind the subapical meristematic zone lies the region of elongation.

Step 2: Cellular Role in Axial Growth
Cells in this zone undergo rapid enlargement and longitudinal elongation, providing the primary mechanical driving force for the longitudinal extension of the root through the soil.

Final Answer: The region of elongation is responsible for the growth of the root in length.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q17 - Distinctive morphological characteristics of plant stem

questiontext.text: Which morphological feature decisively distinguishes a typical stem from a root?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagnostic Anatomy of Stem
The stem forms the ascending axis of the shoot system originating from the embryonic plumule.

Step 2: Key Distinguishing Morphology
Unlike roots, stems possess distinct nodes (where leaves arise) and internodes (the regions between successive nodes), alongside terminal or axillary buds.

Final Answer: The stem is distinguished from the root by bearing nodes and internodes.

answer.text: Complete absence of any branching or lateral appendages

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q18 - Swollen pulvinus leaf base in leguminous plants

questiontext.text: In some leguminous plants, what is the swollen leaf base termed as?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Leaf Base Variations
The leaf base attaches the petiole to the stem node and may bear lateral outgrowths or undergo specialized swelling.

Step 2: Pulvinus Characteristics
In leguminous plants, the leaf base frequently becomes conspicuously swollen into a cushion-like structure termed the pulvinus.

Final Answer: The swollen leaf base in leguminous plants is called the pulvinus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q19 - Mechanical and physiological roles of leaf petiole

questiontext.text: What is the functional significance of a long, thin, flexible petiole in flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Petiole Structure and Function
The petiole connects the lamina to the leaf base, extending the leaf blade outwards into ambient light.

Step 2: Aerodynamic and Cooling Roles
A flexible petiole allows the lamina to flutter in moving air currents, facilitating convective cooling and replenishing fresh carbon dioxide-rich air at the leaf surface.

Final Answer: The petiole allows the blade to flutter in the wind, cooling the leaf and refreshing ambient air.

answer.text: It allows leaf blades to flutter in wind, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface
It converts permanently into a woody thorn to prevent animal grazing
It produces floral ovules through endogenous bud development
It replaces the stem as the primary subterranean storage organ

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q20 - Distribution of reticulate and parallel leaf venation

questiontext.text: How is leaf venation generally distributed across the two major classes of angiosperms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Venation Patterns
When veinlets anastomose to form an interconnected network, venation is reticulate. When veins run parallel along the length of the lamina, it is parallel.

Step 2: Taxonomic Correlation
Dicotyledonous leaves predominantly exhibit reticulate venation, whereas leaves of monocotyledons typically possess parallel venation.

Final Answer: Reticulate venation generally characterizes dicotyledons, while parallel venation characterizes monocotyledons.

answer.text: Reticulate venation is typical of dicotyledons, while parallel venation characterizes monocotyledons
Parallel venation is typical of dicotyledons, while reticulate venation characterizes monocotyledons
Both dicotyledons and monocotyledons possess exclusively parallel venation
Both dicotyledons and monocotyledons possess exclusively reticulate venation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q21 - Position of axillary bud in compound leaves

questiontext.text: Regarding the presence of buds in simple and compound leaves, which statement is factually accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Simple versus Compound Leaf
In simple leaves, the lamina is undivided or its incisions do not reach the midrib. In compound leaves, incisions reach the midrib, creating separate leaflets.

Step 2: Axillary Bud Localization
An axillary bud is consistently found in the axil of the main petiole in both simple and compound leaves; however, an axillary bud never occurs in the axil of individual leaflets.

Final Answer: A bud is present in the axil of the petiole, but never in the axil of leaflets.

answer.text: A bud is present in the axil of the petiole, but is absent in the axil of leaflets
A bud is present in the axil of every single leaflet, but absent at the petiole
Buds are completely absent in both the petiole and the leaflets of compound leaves
Buds are present at both the petiole axil and the tip of every leaflet blade

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q22 - Common rachis axis in pinnately compound leaves

questiontext.text: In a pinnately compound leaf, such as that of neem, the leaflets are arranged on a common axis called the rachis. What does the rachis represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomy of Pinnate Leaves
In pinnately compound leaves, deep incisions partition the blade into multiple distinct lateral leaflets along a central longitudinal axis.

Step 2: Nature of Rachis
This central elongate axis is the rachis, which morphologically represents the midrib of the original leaf.

Final Answer: The rachis of a pinnately compound leaf represents the midrib of the leaf.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q23 - Characteristics and examples of alternate leaf phyllotaxy

questiontext.text: In which arrangement does a single leaf arise at each successive node in an alternate manner, as observed in china rose, mustard, and sunflower?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Phyllotaxy Classification
Phyllotaxy defines the geometric arrangement of leaves along a shoot axis or stem node.

Step 2: Alternate Pattern
When a single leaf originates at each node sequentially on alternating sides of the stem, it is classified as alternate phyllotaxy, as in china rose, mustard, and sunflower.

Final Answer: The arrangement with a single leaf at each node in an alternate manner is alternate phyllotaxy.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q24 - Opposite phyllotaxy examples in Calotropis and guava

questiontext.text: A pair of leaves arises at each node and lie opposite to each other in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Opposite Phyllotaxy Definition
When two leaves arise at the same node on diametrically opposite sides of the stem, the arrangement is termed opposite.

Step 2: Representative Genera
Classic examples of opposite phyllotaxy described in flowering plants include Calotropis and guava.

Final Answer: Opposite phyllotaxy occurs in Calotropis and guava.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q25 - Whorled arrangement of leaves in Alstonia

questiontext.text: If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, what is this phyllotaxy termed, and which plant is an example?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Whorled Phyllotaxy Concept
When more than two leaves are produced in a circle or ring around a single node, the pattern is designated as whorled phyllotaxy.

Step 2: Botanical Example
The tree Alstonia displays this distinctive whorled phyllotaxy at each node.

Final Answer: More than two leaves arising at a node form whorled phyllotaxy, as in Alstonia.

answer.text: Pinnate phyllotaxy, as seen in silk cotton

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q26 - Acropetal flower arrangement in racemose inflorescence

questiontext.text: In a racemose inflorescence, how are flowers borne on the floral axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Racemose Shoot Dynamics
In racemose inflorescences, the main floral axis does not terminate in a flower and continues indefinite vegetative-like apical elongation.

Step 2: Succession Pattern
The lateral floral buds are initiated successively such that older flowers are situated toward the base and younger flowers appear toward the growing apex (acropetal succession).

Final Answer: In a racemose inflorescence, flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession on a continuously growing axis.

answer.text: Laterally in an acropetal succession on an axis that continues to grow
Basipetally on an axis terminating in an apical flower
Centripetally on a completely flat, fleshy disc with no lateral buds
Solitarily at the base of underground adventitious rootstocks

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q27 - Radial symmetry in actinomorphic angiosperm flowers

questiontext.text: When a flower can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre, it is actinomorphic. Which group of plants demonstrates this symmetry?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Actinomorphic Symmetry Concept
Actinomorphic flowers exhibit radial symmetry, meaning that two identical halves are produced by cutting across any vertical plane through the central floral axis.

Step 2: Species Examples
Mustard, datura, and chilli are classical examples of actinomorphic flowers.

Final Answer: Mustard, datura, and chilli have actinomorphic flowers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q28 - Bilateral symmetry in zygomorphic flowering plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of plants possess zygomorphic flowers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Zygomorphic Symmetry Concept
Zygomorphic flowers possess bilateral symmetry, meaning they can only be divided into two equal halves along a single, unique vertical plane passing through the center.

Step 2: Species Examples
Pea, gulmohur, bean, and Cassia are standard examples of zygomorphic flowers.

Final Answer: Pea, gulmohur, bean, and Cassia possess zygomorphic flowers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q29 - Asymmetric irregular floral symmetry in Canna

questiontext.text: A flower that cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre is irregular or asymmetric. Which plant exhibits this type of flower?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Asymmetry in Flowers
When a flower lacks any plane of symmetry and cannot be partitioned into two equivalent mirror images, it is described as asymmetric or irregular.

Step 2: Example Identification
Canna is the standard angiosperm example exhibiting asymmetric floral organization.

Final Answer: Canna has asymmetric (irregular) flowers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q30 - Superior ovary orientation in hypogynous flowers

questiontext.text: In a hypogynous flower, what is the position of the gynoecium relative to other floral whorls, and how is the ovary described?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Hypogyny
In hypogynous flowers, the gynoecium occupies the uppermost point on the convex or conical thalamus.

Step 2: Insertion and Superior Ovary
The remaining floral organs (sepals, petals, and stamens) are inserted below the base of the ovary, rendering the ovary superior, as seen in mustard, china rose, and brinjal.

Final Answer: In hypogynous flowers, the gynoecium occupies the highest position and the ovary is superior.

answer.text: Gynoecium occupies the highest position with other parts below it; ovary is superior
Gynoecium is embedded in the thalamus rim at the same level; ovary is half inferior
Gynoecium is situated below the fused thalamus margin; ovary is inferior
Gynoecium is completely absent; the flower possesses only sterile staminodes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q31 - Half inferior ovary in perigynous flowers

questiontext.text: In perigynous flowers, the gynoecium is situated in the centre and other floral whorls are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level. Such flowers with a half inferior ovary are seen in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Perigynous Floral Layout
In perigyny, the thalamus forms a cup-shaped or saucer-shaped receptacle surrounding the gynoecium.

Step 2: Ovary Classification and Plants
Because the stamens, petals, and sepals emerge from the rim of the receptacle at roughly the same height as the ovary, the ovary is designated as half inferior, found in plum, rose, and peach.

Final Answer: Perigynous flowers with half inferior ovaries occur in plum, rose, and peach.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q32 - Inferior ovary condition in epigynous flowers

questiontext.text: Which of the following flowers are epigynous with an inferior ovary, where the margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Epigynous Floral Structure
In epigynous flowers, the receptacle or thalamus margin grows entirely around and fuses with the ovary wall.

Step 2: Insertion of Parts and Examples
The calyx, corolla, and androecium arise from the top of the ovary, resulting in an inferior ovary; this is characteristic of guava, cucumber, and the ray florets of sunflower.

Final Answer: Epigynous flowers with inferior ovaries are found in guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower.

answer.text: Guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q33 - Non overlapping margins in valvate aestivation

questiontext.text: When sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin without overlapping, what is this aestivation called, and where is it observed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Aestivation Definition
Aestivation refers to the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud relative to other members of the same whorl.

Step 2: Valvate Arrangement
When the adjacent margins of the floral leaves lie in close contact without any overlapping edges, the aestivation is valvate, typified by Calotropis.

Final Answer: Valvate aestivation with non-overlapping margins occurs in Calotropis.

answer.text: Twisted aestivation, as seen in china rose

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q34 - Regularly overlapping appendages in twisted aestivation

questiontext.text: If one margin of an appendage overlaps that of the next one and so on in a regular clockwise or anticlockwise sequence, the aestivation is twisted. In which group is this found?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Twisted Aestivation Morphology
In twisted (contorted) aestivation, each petal or sepal has one margin external (overlapping) and the other margin internal (overlapped by the preceding member).

Step 2: Characteristic Examples
This precise regular pattern of overlap is characteristic of china rose, lady's finger, and cotton.

Final Answer: Twisted aestivation occurs in china rose, lady's finger, and cotton.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q35 - Irregular overlapping petals in imbricate aestivation

questiontext.text: In a floral bud, when the margins of sepals or petals overlap one another, but not in any particular direction, what is this aestivation called, and which plants exhibit it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Aestivation Patterns Analysis
In twisted aestivation, overlapping follows a consistent directional progression, whereas in valvate, margins meet without overlapping.

Step 2: Imbricate Characteristics and Genera
When sepals or petals overlap irregularly without a fixed directional orientation, the arrangement is defined as imbricate; this is typically exhibited by Cassia and gulmohur.

Final Answer: Imbricate aestivation with non-directional overlapping occurs in Cassia and gulmohur.

answer.text: Imbricate aestivation, as seen in Cassia and gulmohur
Twisted aestivation, as seen in lady's finger and cotton
Valvate aestivation, as seen in Calotropis and mustard
Vexillary aestivation, as seen in pea and bean

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q36 - Arrangement of petals in vexillary aestivation

questiontext.text: Which description correctly details the arrangement of the five petals in vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation found in pea and bean flowers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Papilionaceous Corolla Architecture
In the family Fabaceae (pea and bean), the corolla comprises five distinct petals forming a specialized butterfly-like shape.

Step 2: Vexillary Petal Hierarchy
The outermost and largest posterior petal, termed the standard (vexillum), overlaps two lateral wing petals (alae), which in turn overlap the two smallest, often partially fused anterior keel petals (carina).

Final Answer: In vexillary aestivation, the largest standard overlaps two lateral wings, which overlap two anterior keel petals.

answer.text: The largest standard petal overlaps two lateral wing petals, which in turn overlap two smallest anterior keel petals
Two anterior keel petals overlap two lateral wing petals, which overlap one posterior standard petal
All five petals overlap each other along one uniform rotational direction
All five petals remain completely separate and meet only at their basal margins without overlap

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q37 - Cohesion of stamens in bundles across angiosperms

questiontext.text: Match the pattern of stamen cohesion with its representative plant correctly:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stamen Cohesion Terminology
Stamens may remain distinct and free (polyandrous) or fuse together by their filaments into bundles (adelphous condition).

Step 2: Comparative Grouping Across Genera
Stamens united into a single central bundle or staminal tube occur in china rose (monoadelphous); stamens united into two distinct bundles occur in pea (diadelphous); and stamens united into more than two bundles occur in citrus (polyadelphous).

Final Answer: Stamens are monoadelphous in china rose, diadelphous in pea, and polyadelphous in citrus.

answer.text: Monoadelphous in china rose, diadelphous in pea, and polyadelphous in citrus
Monoadelphous in pea, diadelphous in citrus, and polyadelphous in china rose
Monoadelphous in citrus, diadelphous in china rose, and polyadelphous in pea
Monoadelphous in mustard, diadelphous in Salvia, and polyadelphous in tomato

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q38 - Variation in stamen filament length within flower

questiontext.text: In certain angiosperms, there is a distinct variation in the length of stamen filaments within the same flower. Which pair of plants demonstrates this feature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Filament Heteromorphism
While stamens in many species have filaments of uniform length, certain families exhibit unequal filament lengths within a single flower.

Step 2: Taxonomic Occurrence
A notable variation in filament length is characteristically observed in Salvia (Lamiaceae) and mustard (Brassicaceae).

Final Answer: Variation in the length of stamen filaments within a flower occurs in Salvia and mustard.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q39 - Adhesion of stamens to petals and perianth

questiontext.text: When stamens adhere to floral envelopes, how are epipetalous and epiphyllous conditions differentiated, and in which plants do they occur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Floral Adhesion Concepts
Adhesion refers to the fusion between members of two different floral whorls.

Step 2: Epipetalous versus Epiphyllous
When stamens fuse with petals, they are epipetalous, as seen in brinjal (Solanaceae). When stamens are attached directly to the undifferentiated perianth segments, they are epiphyllous, as seen in lily (Liliaceae).

Final Answer: Stamens attached to petals are epipetalous (brinjal), whereas stamens attached to perianth are epiphyllous (lily).

answer.text: Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals as in brinjal; epiphyllous stamens are attached to perianth as in lily
Epipetalous stamens are attached to perianth as in brinjal; epiphyllous stamens are attached to petals as in lily
Epipetalous stamens are attached to sepals as in pea; epiphyllous stamens are attached to gynoecium as in citrus
Epipetalous stamens are attached to the pedicel as in mustard; epiphyllous stamens are attached to the bract as in canna

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q40 - Free and fused carpels in angiosperm gynoecium

questiontext.text: How are apocarpous and syncarpous gynoecia distinguished, and which pairs of plants represent these conditions respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Carpellary Fusion Terminology
A multicarpellary pistil can exhibit carpels that either remain completely separate or fuse during floral ontogeny.

Step 2: Apocarpy versus Syncarpy
When multiple carpels remain free from each other, the gynoecium is apocarpous (typified by lotus and rose). When carpels are fused together into a compound pistil, it is syncarpous (typified by mustard and tomato).

Final Answer: Apocarpous gynoecia have free carpels (lotus, rose), whereas syncarpous gynoecia have fused carpels (mustard, tomato).

answer.text: Apocarpous has free carpels as in lotus and rose; syncarpous has fused carpels as in mustard and tomato
Apocarpous has fused carpels as in lotus and rose; syncarpous has free carpels as in mustard and tomato
Apocarpous has a single carpel as in pea; syncarpous has no carpels as in cucumber
Apocarpous has basal ovules as in sunflower; syncarpous has parietal ovules as in Dianthus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q41 - Comparison between marginal and axile placentation types

questiontext.text: Compare marginal and axile placentation based on placenta position, locule number, and plant examples:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Marginal Placentation Structural Features
In marginal placentation, characteristic of monocarpellary unilocular ovaries like pea, the placenta develops as a continuous ridge along the ventral suture bearing two rows of ovules.

Step 2: Axile Placentation Structural Features
In axile placentation, the ovary is multilocular due to true septa, and the ovules are attached to a central axial placenta meeting at the septal junction, as seen in china rose, tomato, and lemon.

Final Answer: Marginal placentation features ovules along the ventral suture (pea), while axile placentation features ovules on a central axis in a multilocular ovary (china rose, tomato, lemon).

answer.text: Marginal placentation has placenta along the ventral suture forming two rows in pea; axile has placenta in a multilocular ovary in china rose, tomato, and lemon
Marginal placentation has ovules on a central axis without septa in pea; axile has ovules on the outer ovary wall in mustard
Marginal placentation develops at the base with one ovule in sunflower; axile has ovules along the dorsal suture in bean
Marginal placentation occurs in multilocular ovaries in lemon; axile occurs in unilocular ovaries with a false septum in Argemone

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q42 - Parietal placentation and false septum formation

questiontext.text: In parietal placentation, where do the ovules develop, and why does the ovary appear two-chambered in mustard and Argemone?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Parietal Placentation Organization
In parietal placentation, ovules are attached directly to the inner surface of the ovary wall or peripheral placental ridges.

Step 2: Role of the False Septum
The ovary is fundamentally one-chambered (unilocular), but in genera like mustard and Argemone, it becomes secondarily two-chambered through the formation of a false internal partition (septum).

Final Answer: In parietal placentation, ovules develop on the inner wall, and the ovary becomes two-chambered due to the formation of a false septum.

answer.text: Ovules develop on the inner wall or peripheral part; the ovary becomes two-chambered due to a false septum
Ovules develop on the central column; the ovary becomes two-chambered due to fusion of floral bracts
Ovules develop at the base of the ovary; the ovary becomes two-chambered due to inward folding of the calyx
Ovules develop along the dorsal suture; the ovary becomes two-chambered due to complete abortion of one carpel

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q43 - Distinction between free central and basal placentation

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly contrasts free central placentation with basal placentation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Free Central Placentation Structure
In free central placentation, ovules arise upon a central column inside a unilocular ovary that completely lacks partitioning septa, as found in Dianthus and Primrose.

Step 2: Basal Placentation Structure
In basal placentation, the placenta is restricted to the base of a unilocular ovary and bears only a single ovule, as observed in sunflower and marigold.

Final Answer: Free central placentation has ovules on a central axis lacking septa (Dianthus, Primrose), whereas basal placentation has a single basal ovule (sunflower, marigold).

answer.text: In free central, ovules are on a central axis without septa (Dianthus, Primrose); in basal, placenta develops at the ovary base with a single ovule (sunflower, marigold)
In free central, ovules develop along the ventral suture (pea); in basal, ovules are in multilocular chambers (lemon)
In free central, ovules develop on the inner peripheral wall (mustard); in basal, ovules are suspended from the top of the ovary (Argemone)
In free central, ovules are attached to a false septum (tomato); in basal, ovules are attached to an elongated rachis (maize)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q44 - Pericarp differentiation in drupes of mango coconut

questiontext.text: Both mango and coconut fruits are drupes. Which statement accurately analyzes their morphological origin and pericarp structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ontogeny of Drupes
Drupes in mango and coconut develop from a monocarpellary superior ovary and typically contain a single seed.

Step 2: Pericarp Tissue Differentiation
In mango, the pericarp differentiates into a thin outer epicarp, a middle fleshy and succulent edible mesocarp, and an inner stony endocarp; in coconut, the mesocarp is uniquely fibrous.

Final Answer: Drupes develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded; mango has a fleshy mesocarp, whereas coconut has a fibrous mesocarp.

answer.text: They develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded; mango has a fleshy mesocarp while coconut has a fibrous mesocarp
They develop from multicarpellary inferior ovaries and are many-seeded; mango has a stony mesocarp while coconut has a fleshy endocarp
They develop from bicarpellary syncarpous ovaries; mango has an edible fibrous epicarp while coconut has an edible stony pericarp
They develop without fertilisation as parthenocarpic fruits with an undifferentiated membranous pericarp

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q45 - Endospermic versus non endospermic dicotyledonous seeds

questiontext.text: Analyze the structural organization and endosperm persistence in dicotyledonous seeds:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dicot Seed Coat Layers
The protective seed coat consists of two layers: an outer thick testa and an inner delicate tegmen, marked by a scar (hilum) and a micropyle pore.

Step 2: Fate of Endosperm
During seed maturation, the endosperm may persist as a nutrient-storing tissue (endospermic seed, as in castor) or be completely consumed by the developing embryo (non-endospermous seed, as in bean, gram, and pea).

Final Answer: The seed coat comprises an outer testa and inner tegmen; castor is endospermic, whereas bean, gram, and pea are non-endospermous.

answer.text: The seed coat consists of an outer testa and inner tegmen; castor seeds are endospermic, whereas bean, gram, and pea seeds are non-endospermous
The seed coat consists of an outer tegmen and inner testa; castor seeds are non-endospermous, whereas bean, gram, and pea seeds are endospermic
The seed coat lacks a hilum and micropyle; all dicotyledonous seeds retain a bulky endosperm at maturity
The seed coat is completely fused with the fruit wall; castor, bean, and pea all lack cotyledons

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q46 - Embryo and endosperm organization in maize seed

questiontext.text: In the monocotyledonous seed of maize, which structural relationships are correct regarding the endosperm and protective embryonic sheaths?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Endosperm Separation in Monocot Seed
In maize grain, the bulky food-storing endosperm is delimited externally from the lateral embryo by a specialized proteinaceous cellular sheath termed the aleurone layer.

Step 2: Protective Sheaths of the Embryonal Axis
Within the small embryo, the short embryonal axis features a plumule enclosed in a protective foliar sheath (coleoptile) and a radicle enclosed in a protective root sheath (coleorhiza).

Final Answer: The proteinous aleurone layer separates the endosperm from the embryo; the plumule is covered by coleoptile and the radicle by coleorhiza.

answer.text: A proteinous aleurone layer separates the bulky endosperm from the embryo; plumule is enclosed in coleoptile and radicle in coleorhiza
A starchy aleurone layer encloses the radicle; the plumule is covered by coleorhiza and the radicle by coleoptile
The seed coat is completely separate from the pericarp; the embryo is enclosed inside two fleshy scutella
The endosperm is completely absent; the radicle directly differentiates into an aleurone sheath without coleorhiza

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q47 - Floral formula and gynoecium characters of Solanaceae

questiontext.text: Which set of floral characters and floral formula accurately defines the family Solanaceae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Solanaceae Floral Anatomy
Solanaceae flowers are bisexual and actinomorphic, possessing 5 united persistent sepals (valvate), 5 united petals (valvate), and 5 epipetalous stamens alternating with petals.

Step 2: Gynoecium and Floral Formula
The gynoecium is bicarpellary, obliquely placed, syncarpous, with a superior bilocular ovary containing a swollen placenta with many ovules on axile placentation; its formula is \(\oplus \; \text{⚥} \; \text{K}_{(5)} \; \text{C}_{(5)} \; \text{A}_5 \; \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\).

Final Answer: Solanaceae has bisexual actinomorphic flowers, epipetalous stamens, bicarpellary superior ovary with swollen axile placenta, and floral formula \(\oplus \; \text{⚥} \; \text{K}_{(5)} \; \text{C}_{(5)} \; \text{A}_5 \; \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\).

answer.text: Bisexual, actinomorphic, valvate persistent calyx, epipetalous stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary with swollen axile placenta; floral formula is \(\oplus \; \text{⚥} \; \text{K}_{(5)} \; \text{C}_{(5)} \; \text{A}_5 \; \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\)

Zygomorphic, vexillary corolla, diadelphous stamens, monocarpellary superior ovary with marginal placentation; floral formula is \(\% \; \text{⚥} \; \text{K}_{(5)} \; \text{C}_{1+2+(2)} \; \text{A}_{(9)+1} \; \underline{\text{G}}_1\)

Actinomorphic, perianth segments in two whorls, epiphyllous stamens, tricarpellary syncarpous superior ovary; floral formula is \(\oplus \; \text{⚥} \; \text{P}_{3+3} \; \text{A}_{3+3} \; \underline{\text{G}}_{(3)}\)

Bisexual, actinomorphic, cruciform corolla, tetradynamous stamens, bicarpellary ovary with false septum; floral formula is \(\oplus \; \text{⚥} \; \text{K}_{2+2} \; \text{C}_4 \; \text{A}_{2+4} \; \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q48 - Economic and medicinal importance of family Solanaceae

questiontext.text: Identify the correct category-wise grouping of economically significant plants belonging exclusively to the family Solanaceae:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Solanaceae Economic Relevance
The family Solanaceae (potato family) includes numerous commercially, agriculturally, and medicinally valuable species.

Step 2: Categorical Classification
Food sources include potato, tomato, and brinjal; chilli serves as a spice; belladonna and ashwagandha yield essential medicines; tobacco is used as a fumigatory; and petunia is cultivated as an ornamental.

Final Answer: Solanaceae encompasses food plants (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicines (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), and ornamental (petunia).

answer.text: Food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamental (petunia)
